scenes.sub: This week's strangest Black Friday deal
lines: One of this week's biggest Black Friday deals on PC memory takes a hundred and ten dollars off.
Last year, a hundred and ten dollars bought the whole kit.
That's the kind of week it was. Prices that went the wrong way, scores that don't agree, and a movie that couldn't get the screens it was built for.
This is Trend Drop Weekly, episode two. Five stories from November twenty-second to the twenty-eighth, and what they actually mean for you.

scenes.sub: Who gets to score a game?
lines: Story one. The best-reviewed game ever, with a user score of five.
GTA 6 launched on November nineteenth with a ninety-nine on Metacritic.
Only one game had ever hit that number before. Ocarina of Time, back in nineteen ninety-eight.
So you'd expect players to agree. Three days later, the user score on the same site was sitting at about five out of ten.

scenes.sub: Metacritic: anyone • PS Store: owners only
lines: Here's the detail most of the backlash videos skipped.
Anyone can rate a game on Metacritic. You don't have to own it. You don't even have to play it.
Thousands of negative ratings showed up within a day of launch.
On the PlayStation Store, only people who bought the game can rate it.

scenes.sub: ~170K owner ratings on the PS Store
lines: There, about a hundred and seventy thousand owners give it four point eight four out of five.
On a ten-point scale, that's roughly nine point seven.
So the people who paid for it rate it close to the critics. The five comes from a site with no ownership check.
That doesn't mean every complaint is fake.
The game targets thirty frames per second on consoles, with no performance mode, and plenty of real players noticed.
But a thirty frames complaint and a five out of ten are very different claims.
Which brings us to the money. Because this week, the thing getting more expensive wasn't the games. It was the hardware.

scenes.sub: Check who's rating before you trust a score
lines: Why does this matter if you haven't bought it yet?
Because the next time you see a user score, the first question is who's allowed to leave one.
A store that only lets buyers rate is a better signal than a site where anyone can type a number.

And remember the scale. Take-Two says it sold thirty-two and a half million copies before launch day even started. A few thousand angry ratings are loud, but they're a tiny slice of the people actually playing.
Story two. The Black Friday where hardware got pricier.
Consoles used to get cheaper with age. The PS4 dropped fifty dollars two years after launch.
The PS5 went the other way. The Digital Edition launched at three ninety-nine in twenty twenty.
Today it lists at five ninety-nine.
And Sony's best PS5 deal this Black Friday is a refurbished one, at four ninety-nine. That's still a hundred dollars more than a brand new one cost in twenty twenty.
And higher prices have a cost for Sony too.
In May, US PS5 unit sales fell fifty-eight percent from a year earlier, according to Circana. The worst May for PlayStation hardware since two thousand.
The PS5 Pro went from six ninety-nine to eight ninety-nine. So the console that's supposed to make GTA 6 look its best now costs about as much as a decent gaming PC used to.

scenes.sub: 32GB DDR5 kit: 2025 low vs Black Friday 2026
lines: PC memory is worse.
A thirty-two gigabyte DDR5 kit sold for under ninety dollars in twenty twenty-five.
This Black Friday, the deals start around four hundred and forty. About five times as much.
And one of the biggest discounts, a hundred and ten dollars off a Corsair kit, is more than the entire kit cost last year.

scenes.sub: A deal is only a deal vs the old price
lines: Here's the trap. A Black Friday tag shows you a discount off today's list price.
When the list price itself has gone up five times, a big red discount can still be the most you've ever paid.
Engadget found the same thing last year: plenty of Black Friday RAM specials weren't actually cheaper than the regular price had been.
So the number to compare isn't the discount. It's what the same part cost a year ago.

scenes.sub: Memory makers sell to data centers first
lines: So why? The same reason shows up in both stories.
Memory makers are selling to AI data centers first, and reporting ties Sony's price hikes to the same memory squeeze.
SK Hynix's own CEO expects the worst of the shortage in twenty twenty-seven, with demand ahead of supply past twenty thirty.
So if you're waiting for a cheap upgrade, the companies making the chips are telling you it isn't coming soon.
Story three. The shoppers who brought a robot.

scenes.sub: Store visits from AI chatbots, Black Friday 2025
lines: Last Black Friday, store visits that came from AI chatbots jumped over eight hundred percent, according to Adobe's data.
This year it's climbing again. Up about a hundred and twenty-seven percent from November first to the twenty-second.
And Adobe expects Black Friday itself to bring in about twelve point nine billion dollars online.
To put that in context, Black Friday twenty twenty-five brought in about eleven point eight billion dollars online.
This year's forecast is up about nine percent.
And Cyber Monday is still the bigger day. Last year it hit about fourteen and a quarter billion.
So shoppers have a new tool for finding deals. Did the deals get bigger?
No. Adobe's forecast for the deepest electronics discount this year is up to thirty percent. Last year it was thirty point one.
A chatbot can find the deal faster. It can't make it bigger.
One more thing worth knowing. These numbers come from Adobe, which measures stores that use its own software. That's a big sample, but it's not every store.
Story four. Spoiler-free. The Avengers movie that can't get an IMAX screen.
Infinity War and Endgame were the first Hollywood features shot entirely on IMAX digital cameras.
Avengers: Doomsday opens December eighteenth. And in the US, it won't be in IMAX at all.
Dune: Part Three opens the same night and holds US IMAX screens for three weeks.

scenes.sub: Presales on Disney's own premium screens
lines: So Disney built its own answer. It's called Infinity Vision, a premium-screen label it announced in April, covering formats like Dolby, 4DX and ScreenX.
Did losing IMAX hurt? Not so far. Presales made sixteen and a half million dollars on the first day.
And reportedly, more than seventy percent of its first fifty million in presales came from those Infinity Vision screens.

scenes.sub: Infinity Vision on presale day one
lines: That first sixteen and a half million came from roughly a thousand premium screens.
For comparison, the whole point of IMAX was always that it's the biggest, best screen in the building.
Disney is betting that a big Avengers movie can make its own label feel just as special.

scenes.sub: Does the format sell the ticket, or the movie?
lines: So the franchise that helped make IMAX a selling point is now proving it might not need IMAX at all.
Which is a nice setup for the last story. Because over Thanksgiving, we found out what really sells a ticket.
Story five. Thanksgiving at the box office.
The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping opened to a hundred and nineteen million last weekend.
In its second week, over the five-day holiday, it's projected at about eighty-five million.
Disney's new original, Hexed, which reportedly cost over two hundred million dollars, is tracking around thirty-five.
Here's the surprising part. Audiences liked both movies the same.
Hexed got an A-minus CinemaScore. Sunrise on the Reaping got an A-minus too, according to Gold Derby.
And critics scored them within a few points of each other.
And it's a pattern. Disney's last three original Thanksgiving movies, Strange World, Wish and Encanto, opened to about ninety million dollars combined.
Moana 2, a sequel, opened to two hundred and twenty-five million on its own.
Same studio. Same holiday. It's not the movie that's losing. It's the name on the poster.
These are still projections. Sunday's numbers can move.
But here's the twist that should keep Disney from panicking.
Encanto opened to about forty million over the same holiday in twenty twenty-one. Soft.
Then it hit Disney Plus, and a song from it went to number one on the Billboard Hot 100.
Wish didn't get that second life. It opened to thirty-one point six million on a reported budget of around a hundred and seventy-five million.
So Hexed's real test might not be this weekend at all. It might be streaming.
Quick hits.
The Avengers: Doomsday final trailer reached about forty-two million views and sat at number two on US YouTube trending this week, surrounded by breakdown videos.
Focker-in-Law, with a ninety million dollar budget and a twenty-eight percent on Rotten Tomatoes, still out-earned Hexed on Thanksgiving Day.
And the backdrop to all of it. Take-Two says GTA 6 sold three point seven nine billion dollars on day one. That's more than Endgame made in its entire run in theaters.
Cyber Monday is November thirtieth, so expect the deal numbers to keep coming.

scenes.sub: This week, the label beat the thing
lines: So here's the week's verdict.
Again and again, the label beat the thing itself.

A score from people who never played the game. A discount off a price that went up five times. An IMAX logo the movie, so far, hasn't needed. And a poster with a familiar name on it, beating a movie audiences liked just as much.
If there's one habit worth keeping from this week, it's this. Before you trust a number, ask who made it, and what they'd want you to believe.
Which story surprised you most? Tell us in the comments.
And subscribe for next week's drop.
